# A Small Business Guide to Growth Hacking

Written by [Matt Pelkey](https://www.ondeck.com/author/mpelkey)

April 22, 2026 • 6 minute read

 [![Share to Facebook](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/email-assets.enova.com/OnDeck/frontend-assets/icons/share-facebook.svg)](http://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.ondeck.com%2Fresources%2Fgrowth-hacking&title=A+Small+Business+Guide+to+Growth+Hacking)[![Share to Twitter](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/email-assets.enova.com/OnDeck/frontend-assets/icons/share-twitter.svg)](http://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.ondeck.com%2Fresources%2Fgrowth-hacking&text=A+Small+Business+Guide+to+Growth+Hacking)

[Insights and Stories](https://www.ondeck.com/resources/category/insights-and-stories)

![A small business guide to growth hacking](https://www.ondeck.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/5/2022/12/Header_A-Small-Business-Guide-to-Growth-Hacking.png)

Every business has to start somewhere, whether a Silicon Valley tech start-up coding [from a garage](https://www.businessinsider.com/google-apple-hp-microsoft-amazon-started-in-garages-photos-2019-12?r=US&IR=T) or a local store selling to its first customers. 2021 was a record year for new companies, with [Census Bureau](https://www.census.gov/econ/bfs/index.html?) data reporting nearly 5.4 million new establishments. Yet [one in 12 go on to close](https://advocacy.sba.gov/2018/05/01/why-do-businesses-close/), many as a result of low sales. Founders know they need to grow their organization in order to survive, but how can they achieve this in today’s highly competitive commercial environment?

The term [‘growth hacking’](https://www.startup-marketing.com/where-are-all-the-growth-hackers/) was first used by Sean Ellis in 2010, who was responsible for scaling some of Silicon Valley’s best-known ventures, including [Dropbox](https://www.theflyy.com/blog/dropbox-referral-program-a-case-study-of-3900-percent-growth-in-15-months) and [Eventbrite](https://fortune.com/2014/03/13/exclusive-eventbrite-joins-1-billion-club/). For ambitious startups, it can be a challenge to scale their operations. Still, Ellis argues that businesses should actively employ people whose sole focus is to scale operations quickly and effectively.

Many of these ‘growth hackers’ have found success with creative and experimental marketing strategies which aim to generate hype around the business and quickly build a solid customer base. However, this shouldn’t come at the expense of conventional marketing strategies. The Small Business Association advises that companies worth less than $5m invest [around 8% of their revenue](https://blog.hubspot.com/marketing/marketing-budget-percentage) in promoting themselves to achieve growth.

While this might seem daunting, there is plenty that businesses can learn from companies that have hacked their way to rapid growth. That’s why [OnDeck](https://www.ondeck.com/) has created a Small Business Guide to Growth Hacking, with real-life examples to help your organization adopt more creative [marketing](https://www.ondeck.com/resources/small-business-marketing) and level up.

## How to Hack the Marketing Funnel for Business Growth

So how does a business ‘hack’ its way to meaningful growth? Adopting bold strategies can seem daunting at first, but they can help your business quickly reach a wider audience. The [main advantage](https://digitalmarketinginstitute.com/blog/growth-hacking-simple-tips-for-scaling-your-business) many startups have on their side is their marketing can be far more agile than a large organization with established processes, meaning they can quickly pursue other tactics if one fails to generate growth.

While many successful strategies are experimental in nature, they still require an understanding of how it targets various stages of the marketing funnel. Many growth hackers use the [‘Pirate Funnel’](https://growwithward.com/aaarrr-pirate-funnel/) and will aim to target at least one core aim. These are:

*   **Awareness** — How many people a business reaches.
*   **Acquisition** — How many people visit your website or storefront.
*   **Activation** — How many people engage with your business.
*   **Retention** — How many people come back and deal with your business again.
*   **Revenue** — When people start paying for your products and services.
*   **Referral** — How many people tell others about your business.

When growth hackers are looking for ways to scale their business, they will identify and target at least one of these areas, in contrast to an integrated marketing strategy that focuses on all stages of the funnel. To better understand how growth hacking can help your business, we’ve created this helpful guide with seven proven strategies to help your organization unlock its potential.

![Infographic tips for small business growth](https://www.ondeck.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/5/2023/02/A-Small-Business-Guide-to-Growth-Hacking_IG-1.png)

[_Click here to see the image in full size_](https://www.ondeck.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/5/2023/02/A-Small-Business-Guide-to-Growth-Hacking_IG-1.png)

## What types of business loans are good for marketing campaigns?

Marketing often requires upfront investment before you see results. The right type of [small business loan](https://www.ondeck.com/small-business-loans) can help you launch campaigns, manage timing gaps and scale what’s working — without disrupting your day-to-day cash flow.

### Business Term Loan

A [business term loan](https://www.ondeck.com/business-term-loan) provides a lump sum of capital that you repay over a set period. This can be a good option if you’re planning a larger, one-time marketing investment. For example, you might use a term loan to:

*   Launch a major advertising campaign
*   Redesign your website or brand assets
*   Invest in a full-scale product launch

Because payments are predictable, term loans can make it easier to budget for long-term marketing initiatives.

### Short-Term Loans

[Short-term loans](https://www.ondeck.com/short-term-loans) are a type of business term loan that is designed to be repaid quickly, often within a few months to a year. They can be useful when you need fast access to funds for immediate marketing opportunities. You might consider a short-term loan if you want to:

*   Take advantage of a limited-time advertising opportunity
*   Boost seasonal promotions
*   Quickly test a new marketing channel

This option works best when you expect a relatively quick return on your investment.

## What is growth hacking?

Growth hacking, coined in 2010 by Sean Ellis (GrowthHackers cofounder), is a strategy that combines digital marketing, web and product development, and engineering to grow online businesses with limited budgets quickly. Growth hackers take a scientific approach to test and improve customer acquisition and retention strategies.

![Icon representing dynamic ads](https://delivery-p143253-e1476319.adobeaemcloud.com/adobe/assets/urn:aaid:aem:22318604-4b93-487e-9f6f-1e73fbb9d29e/as/growth-hacking-learn-more-what-is-growth-hacking-icon-dsk-v01.png?width=640&preferwebp=true)

## Traditional marketing vs. growth hacking

Traditionally, growth hacking was a startup function for scaling a business at little to no cost. For example, LinkedIn encouraged its early users to invite colleagues via email to join their online professional network for free. Strategic product development, partnerships, and digital ads have led to it having over one Billion users worldwide. 

Dropbox used a similar growth hacking strategy by offering additional online storage space as a reward for referrals.

# Growth Hacking for Small Businesses in Mexico and San Diego: A Practical Guide

By **Kevin Villatoro Burgos** · Updated: November 3, 2026

**Short answer:** Growth hacking (or growth marketing) is a way to grow through small, fast, measured experiments across the whole funnel: attract, convert, sell, retain and earn referrals. For a small business it isn’t about tricks — it’s about choosing one metric, testing one idea at a time, measuring with real data and keeping what works.

Large companies have data teams and budgets to make mistakes. A small business in Tijuana or San Diego rarely does. That’s why the growth approach fits small businesses so well: it forces evidence-based decisions, small spend per test and fast learning. This guide explains how it works and how we apply it at Iskali with businesses across the border region.

## What is growth hacking and how is it different from traditional marketing?

Traditional marketing usually focuses on acquisition: a campaign, an ad, an event. Growth hacking looks at the entire funnel and asks where today’s bottleneck is. Sometimes the problem isn’t getting more visits — it’s a long form, a WhatsApp nobody answers on time, or customers who buy once and never come back.

Growth hacking and growth marketing are used almost interchangeably. The practical difference is emphasis: “hacking” suggests creative low-cost ideas; “marketing” suggests a continuous, structured process. A small business benefits most from the second: a method you repeat every week, designed to scale as the business grows.

## How does the experiment cycle work?

1.  **Pick one main metric.** For example, qualified leads per week or closed sales per month. Just one, so the whole team pushes in the same direction.
2.  **Find the bottleneck.** Review your funnel: visits, contacts, appointments, sales, repeat purchases. Where do the most people drop off?
3.  **Write hypotheses.** “If we reply on WhatsApp in under 10 minutes, more leads will book an appointment.”
4.  **Prioritize.** Score each idea by expected impact, confidence and ease. Start with the cheap, fast ones.
5.  **Test one thing at a time** for a defined period, with a comparison group when possible.
6.  **Measure and decide.** If it works, it becomes a process. If not, document what you learned and move to the next one.

## What drives small business growth?

Marketing experiments work best when the business has healthy foundations. These are the factors that matter most:

*   **Customer understanding:** what they need, how they search, what objections they have and which language they prefer — key at the border.
*   **Continuous experimentation:** testing channels, messages and offers instead of repeating the same thing.
*   **Reliable data:** without a CRM or an organized sheet you know which channel brings clicks, not which brings sales.
*   **Cross-team collaboration:** marketing, sales and customer service should share the same information and the same metric.
*   **Talent and adaptability:** a small team that learns fast has an edge over large, slow companies.
*   **Financing and cash flow:** growth costs money; cheap experiments help you invest only in what has already proven to work.
